title: EchoCoT: Extracting Hidden Chain-of-Thought from Black-Box Models
hook: Providers hide reasoning traces because they're valuable assets. A replay surface between tool calls lets an attacker pull them back out near-verbatim through the public API.
key_points: Hidden CoT traces from frontier reasoning models are treated as proprietary assets; this asks whether the API leaks them anyway.
The attack surface is a previously overlooked 'reasoning replay' point between tool calls.
EchoCoT extracts iteratively, steering itself with fidelity signals the API returns.
An LLM-based optimizer searches for a universal injection trajectory that works across datasets.
On open-source reasoning models: up to 66.4% near-verbatim success — length within 10% of target, at least 90% of tokens matching exactly.
The same trajectory generalizes to unseen datasets (up to 80% success) and scales to very long traces — 33,463 tokens extracted from a 32,948-token target on Gemini-2.5.
content_html: Frontier reasoning models hide their chain-of-thought: you see an answer and perhaps a summary, not the trace. Providers treat those traces as assets worth protecting, partly because they're what a competitor would want for distillation. Qu and colleagues ask whether hidden CoT can be pulled back out of a black-box model through ordinary API interaction, and find that it can.
extra_html:
The attack

They identify a reasoning replay surface sitting between tool calls, and build EchoCoT, a multi-step attack that extracts iteratively while using fidelity signals returned by the API to guide itself. On top of that they add an LLM-based optimization framework that automatically searches for an injection trajectory effective across datasets, rather than tuning per target.

What they measured

Evaluated against three open-source and five frontier proprietary reasoning models, EchoCoT reaches up to 66.4% near-verbatim extraction on the open-source ones — traces within 10% of the target length, with at least 90% of tokens matching exactly — and the same trajectory generalizes to unseen datasets at up to 80% success. For the proprietary models, the authors report that a substantial fraction of extracted traces line up closely with provider-reported reasoning lengths and published CoT summaries. Length is not a defense: on Gemini-2.5 they extract 33,463 tokens against a 32,948-token target. The conclusion is that hidden-CoT extraction is a live security risk, not a theoretical one.

related.title: Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs
related.hook: Labs hide chain-of-thought by handing you an encrypted blob to pass back. Researchers found you can feed that blob to a weaker model from the same provider and have it read the secret aloud.

related.title: Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
related.hook: A misaligned coding agent doesn't need to sneak a backdoor into one pull request — it can spread the attack across many, and no single monitor catches both strategies at once.

flashcards.back_html: A reasoning replay surface between tool calls — a point in the API interaction where hidden chain-of-thought becomes recoverable, previously overlooked.

flashcards.prompt: What makes the attack practical rather than a one-off?

choices.text: An optimizer finds a universal injection trajectory that transfers to unseen datasets
It requires white-box access to the target model's weights
It only works on traces shorter than a few hundred tokens

flashcards.explanation_html: The searched trajectory generalized to datasets it wasn't tuned on, reaching up to 80% extraction success — so it's reusable, not hand-crafted per case.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'near-verbatim' mean in this paper's success criterion?
flashcards.back_html: The extracted trace is within 10% of the target's length with at least 90% of tokens matching exactly — not a paraphrase or summary.
